elements.content: Communication Goal: I can tell the time, talk about days and routines, describe a workday, and compare lifestyles.

Lesson overview:
- Level: A0-A1 General English
- Unit: Inspired Module 3. Daily Rhythm
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: Daily Rhythm
- Materials: Clock visuals, weekly calendar grids, profile cards, frequency line.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• tell the time and use at/on/in
• describe a weekday routine
• talk about another person's routine and compare habits

Prior learning: Recycles time expressions and daily objects.

Quick retrieval task: which words or phrases do you remember?
Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (15 items):

wake up — to stop sleeping. Example: I wake up at seven.
get up — to leave your bed. Example: I get up at seven fifteen.
breakfast — the first meal of the day. Example: I have breakfast at eight.
work — a job or activity you do. Example: I work in an office.
lunch — a meal in the middle of the day. Example: I have lunch at one.
finish — to end. Example: I finish work at six.
evening — the later part of the day. Example: Good evening, Mrs Brown.
Monday — the first day of the working week. Example: I start work at nine on Monday.
Tuesday — the second day of the working week. Example: We have a call on Tuesday.
Friday — the last day of the working week. Example: I finish early on Friday.
o'clock — used to say a full hour. Example: It is seven o'clock.
half past — thirty minutes after the hour. Example: It is half past seven.
commute — to travel to and from work. Example: I commute by metro.
metro — a city train system. Example: I take the metro to work.
on time — not early and not late. Example: I am always on time.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• What time is it? — It's half past eight. (asking and telling the time)
• I wake up at seven and check messages. (morning routine)
• We have a call at ten on Tuesday morning. (scheduling)
• She works from home three days a week. (third-person routine)
• He has coffee at eight and leaves at nine. (third-person routine)
• I usually cook dinner, but I sometimes order food. (frequency and contrast)
• Are you free on Wednesday afternoon? (asking about availability)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'to stop sleeping'?
Which word means 'to leave your bed'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.
Pronunciation Focus: Third-person -s endings and time stress

works /wɜːks/ — voiceless /s/ ending
goes /ɡəʊz/ — voiced /z/ ending
finishes /ˈfɪnɪʃɪz/ — extra /ɪz/ syllable
usually /ˈjuːʒuəli/ — four syllables
Listen and repeat:
She works from home. He goes to the office. She finishes at six. I usually take the metro.

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts, and things that happen regularly.

Form:
Present simple: I / You / We / They + verb. He / She / It + verb + -s. Negative: don't / doesn't + verb. Question: Do / Does + subject + verb?

Examples:
• I work in a school.
• She works in a hospital.
• We don't work on Sunday.
• Does he drink coffee?
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
He ___ tea every morning.
They ___ in a hospital.
She ___ like coffee.
___ you work here?
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I ... (work / study / live) in ...
• He ... (work / study / live) in ...
• They ... (don't / doesn't) ... on Sunday.
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• What do you do every day?
• Where does your best friend work or study?
• Do you drink coffee in the morning?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences about your daily routine.
• Write three sentences about a family member's routine.
Reading: Daily Rhythm

Marcus is an early bird. He wakes up at half past six and makes coffee. He starts work from home at eight. At one, he has lunch and goes for a short walk. He usually finishes at five, and he always goes to the gym on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Priya is a night owl. She gets up at nine thirty and starts work at noon. She finishes late, usually at half past ten at night.
Who wakes up early?
Who finishes work late?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Do you have time for a project call on Tuesday?
B: On Tuesday morning I have client meetings from nine to twelve. What about Tuesday afternoon at two?
A: Sorry, I'm busy at two. Are you free on Thursday morning?
B: Thursday morning is good. I'm free at ten.
A: Ten on Thursday works for me.
When is the meeting?
Why not Tuesday at two?
Speaking task: Compare your weekly schedules. Find two free slots for a coffee and a project call.

• What time do you wake up?
• What do you do on Monday morning?
• How do you get to work?
• How often do you exercise?
• Are you an early bird or a night owl?
Role-play: You are colleagues. Find a time for a call this week and confirm the day, time, and length.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write five sentences about your weekday routine with times, days, and one frequency adverb.
Model: I wake up at ... On Monday, I ... I usually ... I never ...
